**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who knows elementary probability and Fourier analysis, has perhaps never trained a neural network, and wants to understand why a modern camera can photograph a dark room.

**Empirical first**: add Gaussian noise of standard deviation 20 to a 256 × 256 grey crop of the `china.jpg` image shipped with scikit-learn, and the PSNR falls to 22.1 dB; the best Gaussian blur recovers only 24.6 dB, while sliding-window DCT thresholding reaches 26.8 dB, non-local means 27.0 dB and a two-step NL-Bayes 27.8 dB (code in ch. 4–6). Why do these principles rank this way, and what does a trained network add?

The course studies one of the oldest problems of signal processing: separating a signal from its noise. It follows the history of the solutions — Fourier and Gaussian models, transform thresholding, self-similarity, Bayesian patch models — and then trains neural denoisers and compares both families on the same images. The common object is the image *patch*. Related MVA pages: [Sub-Pixel Image Processing](../s1-sub-pixel-image-processing/index.html) shares the sampling theory, [Mathematical Models for Digital Photography](../s1-digital-photography/index.html) the camera noise, and [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) the networks.

### What you will be able to do

-   Explain how an image is sampled, what aliasing is, and compute with the 2D discrete Fourier and cosine transforms.
-   Manipulate Gaussian vectors: affine images, conditioning, the norm of white noise, Stein's lemma.
-   Model the noise of a camera (Gaussian, Poisson, signal dependent), stabilise its variance and estimate its level from a single image.
-   Derive the Wiener filter and the MMSE estimator, and state when a linear filter is optimal.
-   Implement and analyse thresholding in an orthonormal basis, sliding-window DCT denoising and its multiscale version.
-   Implement non-local means and explain the statistics of patch distances and the structure of the space of patches.
-   Derive NL-Bayes and BM3D as empirical Wiener filters on groups of similar patches.
-   Build, train and evaluate a convolutional denoiser in PyTorch, knowing why the L2 loss learns the conditional expectation.
-   Prove that a sliding-window transform-thresholding denoiser is a shallow convolutional network, and read a bias-free network as an adaptive linear filter.
-   Design a fair comparison of denoisers: metrics, paired statistics, noise mismatch, real noise.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com states three objectives: explore the structure of images at the level of *patches* — small image extracts, processed both by neural networks and by recent image processing, whose currently understood size ranges from about 8 × 8 = 64 to 60 × 60 = 3600 pixels; apply this structure to a fundamental problem that requires understanding it, image denoising; and compare image processing designed by humans with image processing learned by deep neural networks.

The description recalls that the separation of noise and signal was already the key problem of Shannon's *Mathematical Theory of Communication*, that denoising approaches identified since the 1970s group into a handful of "denoising principles", and that since 2016 neural denoisers have started to outperform, slightly, the human-made algorithms, with inner workings not yet fully understood. Each session combines a course and online experiments on IPOL.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: elementary probability, Fourier analysis and differential calculus; deep learning is introduced from scratch. It is a **Modelling** course of semester 1, with 5 ECTS and 30 h (20 h of lectures and 10 h of tutorials).

-   **Preparation** — the refreshers [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (Gaussian vectors, conditional expectation), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (spectral theorem, gradients) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (the code of every chapter).
-   **Related courses of semester 1** — [Sub-Pixel Image Processing](../s1-sub-pixel-image-processing/index.html) (sampling and interpolation), [Mathematical Models for Digital Photography](../s1-digital-photography/index.html) (camera pipeline and noise), [The Machine Intelligence of Images](../s1-machine-intelligence-images/index.html), [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) and [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html).
-   **Courses of semester 2 that build on it** — [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html), [Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis](../s2-dl-image-restoration-synthesis/index.html), [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html), [Diffusion and Multiscale Models in AI](../s2-diffusion-multiscale/index.html) (denoisers are the engine of diffusion models), [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html) and [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Review: probability, linear algebra and calculus** — covariance, the bias–variance split of the error, the conditional expectation as best estimator, orthonormal bases.
-   **Image sampling and the discrete Fourier transform** — the Shannon–Whittaker theorem, aliasing, the 2D DFT and DCT, the spectrum of natural images.
-   **A fast tutorial on Gaussian vectors** — definition, independence, invariance of white noise, conditioning and Stein's lemma.
-   **Noise** — Shannon's channel, camera noise, variance stabilisation, noise estimation, the Wiener filter and the denoising principles.
-   **Multiscale DCT denoising** — thresholding in an orthonormal basis, its oracle risk, sliding-window DCT and the multiscale fix of low-frequency noise.
-   **Image self-similarity and denoising** — neighbourhood filters, non-local means, method noise and the space of patches.
-   **Bayesian patch-based methods** — Gaussian patch models, NL-Bayes, BM3D, Gaussian mixtures and EPLL.
-   **A crash course on deep learning** — networks, the L2 loss and the MMSE estimator, backpropagation, SGD, convolutions, residual learning.
-   **Deep and shallow CNN denoisers** — MLP, DnCNN and FFDNet, the shallow network hidden in DCT denoising, bias-free networks.
-   **Comparison of all denoising methods** — protocols, inherent bounds and what each family teaches the other.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — self-supervision, denoisers as priors and diffusion, video and real noise (self-study).

### How to study this module {#study}

-   Read the chapters in order: each chapter uses only the earlier ones, and ch. 2 (Gaussian vectors) is used everywhere afterwards.
-   After each session, do the exercises listed in its row, then run the code of the chapter and change one parameter (noise level, patch size, threshold) to see its effect.
-   Reproduce the IPOL experiments named in the "IPOL experiment" notes on www.ipol.im: the official weekly report is about such online experiments and needs no programming.
-   The Python blocks use NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn (for its two bundled sample images, `china.jpg` and `flower.jpg`) and PyTorch on CPU; every block runs in less than half a minute on a laptop.
-   Keep a table of PSNR values for the same noisy image across chapters: it becomes the comparison of ch. 9.

## 0. Review: probability, linear algebra and calculus {#ch0}

Every chapter of the course measures an error, averages noisy values or changes basis. This review fixes the notation and proves the three facts used everywhere: covariances transform simply, the error of an estimator splits into bias and variance, and the conditional expectation is the best possible estimator.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Mean and covariance of a random vector]{.tag} Let $X$ be a random vector of $\mathbb{R}^d$ with finite second moment. Its mean is $m = \mathbb{E}[X]$ and its covariance matrix is

$$
C = \mathbb{E}\big[(X - m)(X - m)^\top\big].
$$

The matrix $C$ is symmetric and positive semi-definite, because for every vector $a$ the number $a^\top C a$ equals the variance of $\langle a, X\rangle$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Affine maps]{.tag} If $Y = AX + b$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^k$, then

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y] = Am + b, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(Y) = A\, C\, A^\top .
$$

In particular, the average of $K$ uncorrelated values of variance $\sigma^2$ has variance $\sigma^2 / K$.

::: proof
The mean is linear. Then $Y - \mathbb{E}[Y] = A(X - m)$, so the covariance is the expectation of $A (X - m)(X - m)^\top A^\top$, which is $A C A^\top$. For the average, take $A = (1/K, \dots, 1/K)$ and $C = \sigma^2 I$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Bias–variance decomposition]{.tag} Let $\hat X$ be a random estimator of a fixed vector $x$. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}\|\hat X - x\|^2 = \|\mathbb{E}\hat X - x\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|\hat X - \mathbb{E}\hat X\|^2 .
$$

::: proof
Write

$$
\hat X - x = (\hat X - \mathbb{E}\hat X) + (\mathbb{E}\hat X - x)
$$

and expand the square. The cross term is the expectation of a centred vector against a constant vector, hence zero. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.4 — Averaging three pixels]{.tag} A 1D signal is a step from 0 to 60, observed with noise of standard deviation $\sigma = 20$. Replace each sample by the mean of itself and its two neighbours.

-   Far from the step, the bias is zero and the variance is $400/3 \approx 133.3$.
-   On the two samples next to the step, the mean is off by $60/3 = 20$, a squared bias of 400.

The same filter that divides the noise variance by 3 in flat regions triples the error at the edge. Every denoising method of this course is a way out of this dilemma.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — The conditional expectation is the best estimator]{.tag} Let $X$ and $Y$ be random vectors with $\mathbb{E}\|X\|^2 < \infty$, and write $g(Y) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]$. For every measurable $f$ with $\mathbb{E}\|f(Y)\|^2 < \infty$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\|X - f(Y)\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\|X - g(Y)\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|g(Y) - f(Y)\|^2 .
$$

::: proof
Write $X - f(Y) = (X - g(Y)) + (g(Y) - f(Y))$ and expand.

The cross term is the expectation of $\langle X - g(Y), g(Y) - f(Y)\rangle$. Conditioning on $Y$, the second factor is fixed and the first has conditional mean zero, so the tower property makes the cross term vanish. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: key
[Key result — the minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimator]{.tag}

$$
\arg\min_f \ \mathbb{E}\|X - f(Y)\|^2 = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]
$$
:::

With $X$ the clean image and $Y$ the noisy one, the ideal denoiser is the posterior mean. Chapter 2 computes it for Gaussian images, and ch. 7 shows that a network trained with the square loss approximates it.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — Orthonormal basis, Parseval identity]{.tag} Vectors $e_1, \dots, e_d$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ form an orthonormal basis if $\langle e_k, e_l\rangle = \delta_{kl}$. Then every $x$ decomposes as $x = \sum_k \langle x, e_k\rangle e_k$, and

$$
\|x\|^2 = \sum_{k=1}^d \langle x, e_k\rangle^2 .
$$

The matrix $U$ whose columns are the $e_k$ is orthogonal: $U^\top U = I$. The same holds in $\mathbb{C}^d$ with a unitary matrix.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.7 — Spectral theorem]{.tag} Every real symmetric matrix factors as $C = U \Lambda U^\top$, with $U$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ diagonal and real. If $C$ is a covariance matrix, its eigenvalues are non-negative: they are the variances of $X$ along the orthonormal principal axes (principal component analysis, PCA).
:::

::: note
[Differential calculus used later]{.tag} For a function $u$ of class $C^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, the second-order Taylor formula reads

$$
u(x + y) = u(x) + \nabla u(x) \cdot y + \tfrac12\, y^\top D^2u(x)\, y + o(|y|^2).
$$

It gives the method noise of the Gaussian filter (Proposition 3.9). The chain rule $D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg(f(x))\, Df(x)$ is backpropagation (ch. 7.3).
:::

The following Monte Carlo experiment checks Example 0.4.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.r_[np.zeros(10), 60 * np.ones(10)]                # a step of height 60
sigma, trials = 20.0, 20000
Y = x + sigma * rng.standard_normal((trials, x.size))  # noisy realisations
Xh = (np.roll(Y, 1, 1) + Y + np.roll(Y, -1, 1)) / 3    # 3-pixel moving average
bias2 = (Xh.mean(0) - x) ** 2
var = Xh.var(0)
print("squared bias, samples 8-11:", np.round(bias2[8:12], 1))
print("variance,     samples 8-11:", np.round(var[8:12], 1))
```

The output shows squared biases close to 0, 400, 400, 0 and variances close to 133 on the four samples around the step.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 0
:::

-   Covariances transform as $A C A^\top$; averaging $K$ uncorrelated values divides the variance by $K$.
-   Mean square error = squared bias + variance: smoothing trades one for the other.
-   The best estimator in mean square is the conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]$.
-   Orthonormal bases preserve norms; symmetric matrices diagonalise in such a basis.
::::

## 1. Image sampling and the discrete Fourier transform {#ch1}

A digital image is a finite array of samples of a continuous light field. This chapter says what sampling preserves and what it destroys (aliasing), and builds the two orthonormal bases — the discrete Fourier and cosine transforms — in which signal and noise will be separated.

### 1.1 Band-limited images and the sampling theorem

We use the Fourier transform $\hat u(\xi) = \int u(x)\, e^{-i x \xi}\, dx$ on $\mathbb{R}$; the 2D statements follow by tensor products. A function is *band-limited* to $[-\pi, \pi]$ when $\hat u$ vanishes outside this interval. Sampling means keeping the values $u(k)$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.1 — Poisson formula and aliasing]{.tag} Let $u$ be continuous with $u$ and $\hat u$ integrable and decaying fast enough for the series below to converge absolutely. Then, for every $\xi$,

$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat u(\xi + 2\pi n) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} u(k)\, e^{-i k \xi}.
$$

The right-hand side is the spectrum of the samples. It is the *periodisation* of $\hat u$: the frequencies $\xi + 2\pi n$ fold onto $\xi$.

::: proof
The left-hand side $F(\xi)$ is $2\pi$-periodic. Its Fourier coefficients are

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} F(\xi)\, e^{i k \xi}\, d\xi = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}} \hat u(\xi)\, e^{i k \xi}\, d\xi = u(k),
$$

by gluing the translated intervals and by Fourier inversion. A continuous periodic function with absolutely summable coefficients equals its Fourier series. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.2 — Shannon–Whittaker sampling theorem]{.tag} If $u$ satisfies the assumptions of Proposition 1.1 and is band-limited to $[-\pi, \pi]$, then $u$ is determined by its samples:

$$
u(x) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} u(k)\, \mathrm{sinc}(x - k), \qquad \mathrm{sinc}(t) = \frac{\sin \pi t}{\pi t}.
$$

::: proof
On $[-\pi, \pi]$ only the term $n = 0$ of the periodisation is non-zero, so

$$
\hat u(\xi) = \mathbf{1}_{[-\pi,\pi]}(\xi) \sum_k u(k)\, e^{-ik\xi}.
$$

The inverse Fourier transform of $\mathbf{1}_{[-\pi,\pi]}(\xi)\, e^{-ik\xi}$ is $\mathrm{sinc}(x - k)$. Summing term by term gives the formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When $\hat u$ does not vanish outside $[-\pi, \pi]$, the sampled spectrum mixes several frequencies: this is **aliasing**. In a camera, the blur of the optics and of the sensor area acts as the low-pass filter that limits it.

::: ex
[Example 1.3 — A stripe pattern seen at the wrong frequency]{.tag} For every integer $k$,

$$
\cos(2\pi \cdot 0.7\, k) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 0.3\, k),
$$

because $0.7 = 1 - 0.3$. Stripes of 0.7 cycle per pixel (period 1.43 pixels) are recorded as stripes of 0.3 cycle per pixel (period 3.33 pixels). In 2D this produces the moiré patterns of fabrics and roof tiles.
:::

### 1.2 The 2D discrete Fourier transform

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)]{.tag} For an image $u$ on the grid $\Omega = \{0, \dots, M-1\} \times \{0, \dots, N-1\}$,

$$
\hat u(p, q) = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1} \sum_{l=0}^{N-1} u(k, l)\, e^{-2i\pi \left(\frac{pk}{M} + \frac{ql}{N}\right)} .
$$

The *normalised* DFT divides by $\sqrt{MN}$; it is a unitary map of $\mathbb{C}^{\Omega}$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.5 — Properties of the DFT]{.tag} With $|\Omega| = MN$:

1.  inversion:
    $$
    u(k,l) = \frac{1}{MN}\sum_{p,q} \hat u(p,q)\, e^{2i\pi (pk/M + ql/N)};
    $$
2.  Parseval:
    $$
    \sum_{\Omega} |u|^2 = \frac{1}{MN} \sum_{\Omega} |\hat u|^2;
    $$
3.  convolution: the circular convolution $u \circledast v$ satisfies $\widehat{u \circledast v} = \hat u\, \hat v$;
4.  translation: a circular shift by $(a, b)$ multiplies $\hat u(p,q)$ by $e^{-2i\pi(pa/M + qb/N)}$.

::: proof
All four follow from the orthogonality relation, a geometric sum:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{M-1} e^{2i\pi k (p - p')/M} = M\, \mathbf{1}[p = p' \bmod M].
$$

For the convolution, substitute $(u \circledast v)(k) = \sum_j u(j)\, v(k - j)$ in the definition and change the index $k - j \to k'$; the sum factors. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The DFT treats the image as periodic. The jump between opposite borders creates artificial high frequencies — the bright cross visible in the spectrum of most photographs. Symmetrising the image before the transform removes this jump; this is the cosine transform of Section 1.4.

### 1.3 Trigonometric interpolation and zoom

For an $N$-periodic discrete signal with $N$ odd, the *DFT interpolate* is the trigonometric polynomial

$$
\bar u(x) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{|p| \le (N-1)/2} \hat u(p)\, e^{2i\pi p x / N}.
$$

It is the only trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $(N-1)/2$ that matches the samples. It gives exact sub-pixel translations — multiply $\hat u(p)$ by $e^{-2i\pi p \tau / N}$ — and zooms by zero-padding the spectrum. Its price is ringing (Gibbs oscillations) near sharp edges.

::: note
[IPOL experiment — zoom and aliasing]{.tag} With an image-interpolation demo on www.ipol.im, or in a few lines of NumPy, zoom an image by zero-padding its DFT and by a local interpolation, then subsample it by 2 without filtering. Look for ringing near edges in the first case and for moiré in the last.
:::

### 1.4 The discrete cosine transform

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Discrete cosine transform (DCT-II)]{.tag} The vectors $c_0, \dots, c_{n-1}$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are

$$
c_k(j) = \alpha_k \cos\Big(\frac{\pi k\, (j + 1/2)}{n}\Big), \qquad \alpha_0 = \sqrt{1/n}, \quad \alpha_k = \sqrt{2/n} \ (k \ge 1).
$$

In 2D, the $n^2$ products $c_k(i)\, c_l(j)$ are the atoms of the separable DCT; for $8 \times 8$ patches there are 64.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — The DCT is the eigenbasis of a symmetric matrix]{.tag} Let $L$ be the Laplacian matrix of the path with $n$ vertices: diagonal $(1, 2, \dots, 2, 1)$ and $-1$ on the two neighbouring diagonals. Then

$$
L\, c_k = \big(2 - 2\cos(\pi k / n)\big)\, c_k .
$$

The $n$ eigenvalues are distinct, so the $c_k$ are pairwise orthogonal; with the constants $\alpha_k$, they form an orthonormal basis.

::: proof
Write $\theta = \pi k / n$ and $c(j) = \cos(\theta (j + 1/2))$. For $0 < j < n-1$, the identity $\cos(a + \theta) + \cos(a - \theta) = 2\cos\theta \cos a$ gives

$$
2c(j) - c(j-1) - c(j+1) = (2 - 2\cos\theta)\, c(j).
$$

At $j = 0$ the matrix row reads $c(0) - c(1)$. It equals the same expression because $c(-1) = c(0)$, by parity of the cosine. The case $j = n - 1$ is symmetric.

Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal (Theorem 0.7), and the constants $\alpha_k$ normalise them. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The DCT is the DFT of the image reflected across its borders. There is no artificial jump, so the energy of smooth patches concentrates in few low-frequency coefficients. This *energy compaction* explains its use in JPEG and in the denoisers of ch. 4.

### 1.5 The spectrum of natural images

Measured on large collections, the power spectrum of natural images decays roughly like $|\xi|^{-2}$ (Field, 1987; Ruderman and Bialek, 1994). White noise has a flat spectrum, equal to $\sigma^2$ for the normalised DFT. The signal-to-noise ratio per frequency therefore decreases with $|\xi|$.

::: ex
[Example 1.8 — Where noise wins]{.tag} Model the spectrum by $S(\xi) = A / |\xi|^2$. The signal-to-noise ratio $S(\xi) / \sigma^2$ equals 1 at

$$
|\xi_c| = \sqrt{A} / \sigma .
$$

Doubling $\sigma$ halves the cut-off frequency. Beyond $|\xi_c|$ noise dominates on average — but edges and textures also live there, which is why a fixed low-pass filter cannot be a good denoiser.
:::

The code below builds the $8 \times 8$ DCT, checks its orthonormality, and compares the energy compaction of image patches and of noise patches.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

n = 8
j = np.arange(n)
D = np.sqrt(2 / n) * np.cos(np.pi * np.outer(j, j + 0.5) / n)   # rows = DCT-II atoms
D[0] /= np.sqrt(2)
print("orthonormal:", np.allclose(D @ D.T, np.eye(n)))

u = load_sample_image("china.jpg").mean(axis=2)
H, W = (s - s % n for s in u.shape)
P = u[:H, :W].reshape(H // n, n, W // n, n).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(-1, n, n)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N = 20 * rng.standard_normal(P.shape)                         # white noise, sigma = 20

def energy_in_top6(patches):
    """Mean fraction of the energy carried by the 6 largest of the 64 DCT coefficients."""
    C = np.einsum("ki,pij,lj->pkl", D, patches, D).reshape(len(patches), -1) ** 2
    C.sort(axis=1)
    return (C[:, -6:].sum(1) / C.sum(1)).mean()

print(f"image patches: {energy_in_top6(P - P.mean((1, 2), keepdims=True)):.2f}")
print(f"noise patches: {energy_in_top6(N):.2f}")
print(f"noise variance per DCT coefficient: {np.einsum('ki,pij,lj->pkl', D, N, D).var():.1f}")
```

With their mean removed, image patches put 69 % of their energy in their 6 largest coefficients, against 41 % for noise. The noise variance per coefficient stays 400: an orthonormal transform keeps white noise white (Theorem 2.4).

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::

-   Sampling periodises the spectrum; a band-limited image is recovered exactly by sinc interpolation (Theorem 1.2), otherwise aliasing folds frequencies.
-   The DFT diagonalises circular convolution and translations; it treats the image as periodic.
-   The DCT is the eigenbasis of the path Laplacian, an orthonormal basis without border jumps, with strong energy compaction on image patches.
-   Natural images have a power spectrum decaying like $|\xi|^{-2}$; white noise is flat.
::::

## 2. A fast tutorial on Gaussian vectors {#ch2}

White Gaussian noise is the reference model of the course, and Gaussian models of patches are the core of ch. 6. This chapter collects what we need: the definition, independence, the invariance of white noise under orthonormal transforms, the size of a noise vector, conditioning, and Stein's lemma.

### 2.1 Definition and first properties

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Gaussian vector]{.tag} A random vector $X$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is *Gaussian* if every linear combination $\langle a, X\rangle$ is a real Gaussian variable, possibly constant. We write $X \sim \mathcal{N}(m, C)$ with $m$ its mean and $C$ its covariance.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Characteristic function, affine images, density]{.tag} If $X \sim \mathcal{N}(m, C)$, then for every $t \in \mathbb{R}^d$

$$
\mathbb{E}\, e^{i\langle t, X\rangle} = \exp\big(i\langle t, m\rangle - \tfrac12\, t^\top C\, t\big).
$$

Consequently the law depends only on $(m, C)$, and $AX + b \sim \mathcal{N}(Am + b, A C A^\top)$. If $C$ is invertible, $X$ has the density

$$
p(x) = (2\pi)^{-d/2} \det(C)^{-1/2} \exp\big(-\tfrac12 (x - m)^\top C^{-1} (x - m)\big).
$$

::: proof
The variable $\langle t, X\rangle$ is Gaussian with mean $\langle t, m\rangle$ and variance $t^\top C t$ (Proposition 0.2). Its characteristic function at 1 gives the formula. A characteristic function determines the law.

For the affine image, every linear combination of $AX + b$ is a linear combination of $X$ plus a constant, hence Gaussian. The density follows by the change of variables $X = m + C^{1/2} Z$ with $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Independence equals decorrelation]{.tag} The components of a Gaussian vector are independent if and only if its covariance matrix is diagonal.

::: proof
If $C$ is diagonal, the characteristic function of Proposition 2.2 is a product of functions of each $t_i$, which characterises independence. The converse holds for any random vector. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The hypothesis is that the vector is *jointly* Gaussian. If $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $\varepsilon = \pm 1$ is an independent fair sign, then $Z$ and $\varepsilon Z$ are Gaussian and uncorrelated, but $|Z| = |\varepsilon Z|$: they are not independent.
::::

### 2.2 White noise in an orthonormal basis

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — White noise stays white]{.tag} Let $N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_d)$ and let $U$ be an orthogonal matrix. Then

$$
U N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_d).
$$

The coefficients of white noise in any orthonormal basis are independent $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ variables.

::: proof
By Proposition 2.2, $UN$ is Gaussian, centred, with covariance $U (\sigma^2 I) U^\top = \sigma^2 I$. Independence follows from Proposition 2.3. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This is why every transform method of ch. 4–6 — DCT, wavelets, the PCA of a group of patches — can treat its coefficients one by one with the same noise level $\sigma$. For the normalised DFT of real white noise, every coefficient $\hat n(p)$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}|\hat n(p)|^2 = \sigma^2$, with the conjugate symmetry $\hat n(-p) = \overline{\hat n(p)}$.

### 2.3 The norm of a noise vector

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Concentration of the noise norm]{.tag} If $N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_d)$, then $\|N\|^2 / \sigma^2$ follows a $\chi^2_d$ law, with mean $d$ and variance $2d$. Hence

$$
\frac{\|N\|^2}{d\,\sigma^2} \ \text{has mean } 1 \text{ and standard deviation } \sqrt{2/d}.
$$

::: proof
$\|N\|^2 / \sigma^2$ is a sum of $d$ independent squares $Z_i^2$ of standard Gaussians. Since $\mathbb{E}Z^2 = 1$ and $\mathbb{E}Z^4 = 3$, each square has variance 2, and variances of independent terms add. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.6 — Small and large patches]{.tag} For an $8 \times 8$ patch, $d = 64$ and the relative fluctuation of $\|N\|^2$ is $\sqrt{2/64} = 0.177$. For a $60 \times 60$ patch, $d = 3600$ and it is

$$
\sqrt{2/3600} = 0.024 .
$$

A large patch measures the noise energy almost exactly. This concentration drives the patch comparisons of ch. 5.
:::

### 2.4 Conditioning: the Gaussian denoiser

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.7 — Gaussian conditioning]{.tag} Let $X \sim \mathcal{N}(m, C)$ and $N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$ be independent, and $Y = X + N$. Write $K = C (C + \sigma^2 I)^{-1}$. Given $Y = y$, the law of $X$ is Gaussian:

$$
X \mid Y = y \ \sim\ \mathcal{N}\big(m + K (y - m),\ C - K C\big).
$$

::: proof
The pair $(X, Y)$ is an affine image of $(X, N)$, which is Gaussian by independence; so $(X, Y)$ is a Gaussian vector.

Let $Z = X - m - K(Y - m)$. Its cross-covariance with $Y$ is

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(Z, Y) = C - K (C + \sigma^2 I) = 0 .
$$

The vector $(Z, Y)$ is Gaussian and uncorrelated, hence independent (Proposition 2.3). So $X = m + K(Y - m) + Z$, where $Z$ is centred and independent of $Y$.

Its covariance is $C - KC - CK^\top + K(C + \sigma^2 I)K^\top$. Since $K(C + \sigma^2 I) = C$, the last term is $CK^\top$, leaving $C - KC$. Fixing $Y = y$ gives the conditional law. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — the Wiener estimator of a Gaussian signal]{.tag}

$$
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] = m + C\,(C + \sigma^2 I)^{-1}\,(Y - m)
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Corollary 2.8 — Shrinkage in the principal axes]{.tag} Write $C = U \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_i) U^\top$. In the basis $U$, the MMSE estimator multiplies the $i$-th coefficient of $Y - m$ by

$$
\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_i + \sigma^2},
$$

and its mean square error is $\sum_i \lambda_i \sigma^2 / (\lambda_i + \sigma^2)$.

::: proof
In the basis $U$, the gain is diagonal:

$$
K = U\, \mathrm{diag}\Big(\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_i + \sigma^2}\Big)\, U^\top .
$$

The error covariance $C - KC$ has the eigenvalues $\lambda_i - \lambda_i^2/(\lambda_i + \sigma^2)$, whose sum is the trace. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The estimator keeps the directions where the signal variance dominates the noise and kills the others. All the patch methods of ch. 6 apply this rule with estimated $\lambda_i$.

::: ex
[Example 2.9 — Three principal axes]{.tag} Take $\lambda = (100, 25, 1)$ and $\sigma^2 = 25$.

-   The shrinkage factors are $0.8$, $0.5$ and $1/26 \approx 0.0385$.
-   The error is $20 + 12.5 + 0.96 = 33.46$.
-   The noisy observation itself has error $3 \sigma^2 = 75$.

The Wiener estimator more than halves the error.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
lam, sigma2, n = np.array([100.0, 25.0, 1.0]), 25.0, 200_000
U, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.standard_normal((3, 3)))          # a random orthonormal basis
C = U @ np.diag(lam) @ U.T                                # prior covariance of X
X = rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(3), C, size=n)
Y = X + np.sqrt(sigma2) * rng.standard_normal((n, 3))
K = C @ np.linalg.inv(C + sigma2 * np.eye(3))             # Wiener gain (Theorem 2.7)
print("shrinkage factors:", np.round(np.linalg.eigvalsh(K), 4))
print(f"MSE of Y:        {((Y - X) ** 2).sum(1).mean():.2f}  (theory 75)")
print(f"MSE of K Y:      {((Y @ K.T - X) ** 2).sum(1).mean():.2f}  (theory {np.sum(lam * sigma2 / (lam + sigma2)):.2f})")
```

The simulation returns the factors 0.0385, 0.5, 0.8 and errors of 74.87 and 33.53, against 75 and 33.46 in theory.

### 2.5 Stein's lemma and an unbiased estimate of the risk

:::: prop
[Lemma 2.10 — Gaussian integration by parts (Stein)]{.tag} If $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ and $g$ is absolutely continuous with $\mathbb{E}|g'(Z)| < \infty$, then

$$
\mathbb{E}[Z\, g(Z)] = \sigma^2\, \mathbb{E}[g'(Z)] .
$$

::: proof
The density $\varphi$ of $Z$ satisfies $\varphi'(z) = -z \varphi(z) / \sigma^2$. Integrate $g'(z)\varphi(z)$ by parts; the boundary terms vanish under the integrability assumption. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.11 — Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE; Stein, 1981)]{.tag} Let $Y = x + N$ with $N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_d)$, and let $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ be weakly differentiable with integrable partial derivatives. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}\|f(Y) - x\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\Big[\|f(Y) - Y\|^2 - d\sigma^2 + 2\sigma^2 \operatorname{div} f(Y)\Big].
$$

::: proof
Expand $\|f(Y) - x\|^2 = \|f(Y) - Y + N\|^2$:

$$
\|f(Y) - Y\|^2 + 2\langle f(Y), N\rangle - 2\langle Y, N\rangle + \|N\|^2 .
$$

Here $\mathbb{E}\|N\|^2 = d\sigma^2$, and $\mathbb{E}\langle Y, N\rangle = d\sigma^2$ as well, because $Y = x + N$.

For the remaining term, apply Lemma 2.10 to each coordinate, conditionally on the other coordinates of $N$:

$$
\mathbb{E}[N_i\, f_i(Y)] = \sigma^2\, \mathbb{E}[\partial_i f_i(Y)].
$$

Summing over $i$ gives $2\sigma^2 \mathbb{E}\operatorname{div} f(Y)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The right-hand side involves only $Y$: it estimates the error of a denoiser *without knowing the clean image*. Chapter 4 uses it to choose a threshold, and ch. 8 reads $\operatorname{div} f$ as the trace of a network Jacobian.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::

-   A Gaussian vector is fixed by its mean and covariance; inside it, uncorrelated means independent.
-   White noise has independent $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ coefficients in every orthonormal basis.
-   The squared norm of a $d$-pixel noise patch is $d\sigma^2$ up to a relative error $\sqrt{2/d}$.
-   The posterior mean of a Gaussian signal is the Wiener estimator: shrink each principal coefficient by $\lambda_i / (\lambda_i + \sigma^2)$.
-   SURE estimates the risk of a denoiser from the noisy data alone.
::::

## 3. Noise {#ch3}

Before removing noise we must say what it is. This chapter starts from Shannon's formulation of the problem, follows the noise through a camera, shows how to make it Gaussian and how to measure its level, and ends with the optimal *linear* denoiser and the map of the classical denoising principles.

### 3.1 Signal plus noise: Shannon's problem

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — The denoising problem and its metrics]{.tag} An image $u$ on a grid $\Omega$ is observed as

$$
\tilde u = u + n, \qquad n(i) \ \text{independent}\ \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).
$$

A denoiser $D$ returns $D(\tilde u)$. Its quality is the mean square error

$$
\mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{i \in \Omega} \big(D(\tilde u)(i) - u(i)\big)^2,
$$

reported for 8-bit images as

$$
\mathrm{PSNR} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{255^2}{\mathrm{MSE}} \ \text{dB}.
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.2 — PSNR arithmetic]{.tag} The noisy image itself has $\mathrm{MSE} = \sigma^2$. For $\sigma = 20$:

$$
\mathrm{PSNR} = 10 \log_{10}(65025 / 400) = 22.11 \ \text{dB}.
$$

For $\sigma = 25$ it is 20.17 dB. Halving the root mean square error adds $20 \log_{10} 2 = 6.02$ dB, so a gain of 0.3 dB is a reduction of the RMSE by about 3.4 %.
:::

Shannon's *Mathematical Theory of Communication* (1948) treats a message corrupted by a noisy channel. Its Gaussian case gives the amount of information that noise leaves in each sample.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Capacity of the Gaussian channel (Shannon, 1948)]{.tag} A channel that adds independent $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ noise to inputs of mean power at most $P$ transmits reliably at most

$$
C = \tfrac12 \log_2\Big(1 + \frac{P}{\sigma^2}\Big) \ \text{bits per sample},
$$

and every rate below $C$ is achievable with an error probability tending to zero.

::: proof
*Key step of the converse.* For one use of the channel, the information is $I(X; Y) = h(Y) - h(N)$, where $h$ is the differential entropy. At fixed variance the Gaussian maximises $h$, so $h(Y) \le \frac12 \log_2(2\pi e (P + \sigma^2))$, while $h(N) = \frac12 \log_2(2\pi e \sigma^2)$. Achievability uses random codes; see Cover and Thomas (2006, ch. 9). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For an image whose grey levels have standard deviation 50, observed with $\sigma = 20$, the bound is $\frac12 \log_2(1 + 6.25) = 1.43$ bit per pixel. A denoiser cannot create this missing information. It can only exploit the *redundancy* of images — smoothness, sparsity, self-similarity — exactly as Shannon's codes exploit redundancy to correct errors. Each denoising principle of Section 3.6 is a hypothesis on this redundancy.

### 3.2 Noise in a camera

A pixel counts photons during the exposure. Three sources dominate.

-   **Photon (shot) noise.** The count follows a Poisson law $\mathcal{P}(\lambda)$, with mean and variance $\lambda$. Its signal-to-noise ratio is $\sqrt{\lambda}$: 10 for 100 photons, 100 for 10 000. A dark scene collects few photons and is noisy.
-   **Read-out and thermal noise.** The electronics add a signal-independent, nearly Gaussian noise.
-   **Quantisation.** Rounding to a step $\Delta$ adds an error that is close to uniform.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Quantisation noise]{.tag} An error uniform on $[-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]$ has variance

$$
\frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} t^2\, dt = \frac{\Delta^2}{12}.
$$

::: proof
The integral of $t^2$ over $[-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]$ is $\frac{2}{3}(\Delta/2)^3 = \Delta^3/12$; divide by $\Delta$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

For 8-bit values with $\Delta = 1$, the standard deviation is 0.29 grey level, negligible against $\sigma = 20$.
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Poisson–Gaussian model and noise curve]{.tag} A raw value is modelled as $z = a\, \mathcal{P}(u / a) + \mathcal{N}(0, b)$, with a gain $a$ and a read-out variance $b$ (Foi, Trimeche, Katkovnik and Egiazarian, 2008). Its conditional variance is affine in the signal:

$$
\mathrm{Var}(z \mid u) = a\, u + b .
$$

The function $u \mapsto \mathrm{Var}(z \mid u)$ is the *noise curve* of the sensor.
:::

The camera pipeline then demosaics, white-balances, applies a tone curve and compresses. After these steps the noise is correlated between neighbouring pixels and colour channels, and its variance depends on intensity and frequency. Removing such noise blindly, from a single JPEG image, is the problem addressed by the *Noise Clinic* of Lebrun, Colom and Morel (2015).

### 3.3 Variance stabilisation

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Delta method and the Anscombe transform]{.tag} Let $X$ have mean $\mu$ and variance $v(\mu)$, concentrated around $\mu$. For a smooth $f$,

$$
\mathrm{Var} f(X) \approx f'(\mu)^2\, v(\mu).
$$

Choosing $f' = 1/\sqrt{v}$ makes the variance close to 1. For Poisson counts, $v(\mu) = \mu$ and Anscombe (1948) uses $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x + 3/8}$, whose shift improves the approximation at small counts.

::: proof
Expand $f(X) = f(\mu) + f'(\mu)(X - \mu) + O((X - \mu)^2)$ and take the variance of the first-order term. With $v(\mu) = \mu$, $f'(\mu) = 1/\sqrt{\mu}$ integrates to $2\sqrt{\mu}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The same computation for the affine noise curve gives the *generalised Anscombe transform* $f(z) = \frac{2}{a}\sqrt{a z + \frac38 a^2 + b}$. The usual pipeline stabilises, denoises as if the noise were Gaussian with $\sigma = 1$, and inverts; at low counts, the inverse must be unbiased rather than algebraic (Mäkitalo and Foi, 2011).

### 3.4 Estimating the noise level from one image

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.7 — Median absolute deviation (MAD)]{.tag} If $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, the median of $|Z|$ is $c\,\sigma$ with $c = \Phi^{-1}(3/4) \approx 0.6745$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. Hence the estimator

$$
\hat\sigma = \frac{\mathrm{median}_i\, |d_i|}{0.6745}
$$

computed on high-pass coefficients $d_i$ of the noisy image.

::: proof
$\mathbb{P}(|Z| \le c\sigma) = 2\Phi(c) - 1$, which equals $1/2$ when $\Phi(c) = 3/4$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Take for $d$ the finest diagonal Haar coefficient,

$$
d(k,l) = \tfrac12\big(\tilde u(k,l) - \tilde u(k+1,l) - \tilde u(k,l+1) + \tilde u(k+1,l+1)\big).
$$

Its noise part is $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ by Proposition 0.2, and its signal part vanishes on smooth regions. Edges and textures occupy a minority of pixels, which the median ignores — up to a point.

More accurate methods select the blocks of lowest variance and measure their high-frequency DCT energy, intensity by intensity, which yields a whole noise curve (Colom and Buades, 2013).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# 1) Anscombe: the variance of 2 sqrt(k + 3/8) for Poisson counts k
for lam in [1, 4, 10, 50, 200]:
    k = rng.poisson(lam, 200_000)
    print(f"lambda = {lam:3d}: Var(k) = {k.var():7.2f}, Var(Anscombe) = {(2 * np.sqrt(k + 3 / 8)).var():.3f}")

# 2) MAD estimate of sigma from the finest diagonal Haar coefficients
for name in ["flower.jpg", "china.jpg"]:
    u = load_sample_image(name).mean(axis=2)
    for sigma in [5, 20, 40]:
        f = u + sigma * rng.standard_normal(u.shape)
        d = (f[:-1, :-1] - f[1:, :-1] - f[:-1, 1:] + f[1:, 1:]) / 2   # noise part ~ N(0, sigma^2)
        print(f"{name:10s} sigma = {sigma:2d}: estimate {np.median(np.abs(d)) / 0.6745:5.2f}")
```

The Anscombe variance is 0.72 for $\lambda = 1$ and within 0.4 % of 1 from $\lambda = 4$ on. On the smooth `flower.jpg` the MAD estimates are 5.39, 20.23 and 40.23. On the textured `china.jpg` they are 8.32, 23.26 and 42.47: texture leaks into the high-pass coefficients and biases the estimate upwards, most visibly at low noise.

::: note
[IPOL experiment — noise estimation]{.tag} Run a noise-curve estimator on IPOL on a JPEG photograph and on its raw counterpart if available. Compare the estimated curves for dark and bright intensities with the affine model of Definition 3.5.
:::

### 3.5 Linear filtering, method noise and the Wiener filter

A linear filter $w$ applied to white noise gives a noise of variance $\sigma^2 \|w\|_2^2$ per pixel (Proposition 0.2). A $k \times k$ box filter divides the variance by $k^2$. What it removes from the image is measured by the method noise.

::: def
[Definition 3.8 — Method noise (Buades, Coll and Morel, 2005)]{.tag} The method noise of a denoiser $D_h$ with parameter $h$ is the difference $u - D_h(u)$. A good denoiser has a method noise that looks like noise and contains no structure of the image.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.9 — Method noise of the Gaussian filter]{.tag} Let $u$ be of class $C^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with bounded second derivatives, and $G_h$ the Gaussian kernel with standard deviation $h$ on each axis. Then

$$
u - G_h * u = -\frac{h^2}{2}\, \Delta u + o(h^2).
$$

::: proof
$G_h * u(x) = \mathbb{E}[u(x - Y)]$ with $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, h^2 I_2)$. By the Taylor formula of ch. 0,

$$
u(x - Y) = u(x) - \nabla u(x) \cdot Y + \tfrac12\, Y^\top D^2 u(x)\, Y + o(|Y|^2).
$$

The first-order term has mean zero, and $\mathbb{E}[Y_i Y_j] = h^2 \delta_{ij}$ makes the second-order term $\frac{h^2}{2}\Delta u(x)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The Gaussian filter removes the Laplacian of the image: edges, corners and textures. No choice of $h$ escapes the bias–variance dilemma of Example 0.4.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.10 — Wiener filter]{.tag} Let $F$ be the normalised 2D DFT. Assume $u$ is a periodic stationary Gaussian field with mean $m$ and covariance $F^* \mathrm{diag}(S) F$, where $S(p,q) \ge 0$ is its power spectrum, and let $n$ be white Gaussian noise. Then the MMSE estimate is

$$
\mathbb{E}[u \mid \tilde u] = m + F^* \mathrm{diag}\Big(\frac{S}{S + \sigma^2}\Big) F\, (\tilde u - m).
$$

::: proof
Apply Theorem 2.7 with $C = F^* \mathrm{diag}(S) F$. Since $F$ is unitary, $C + \sigma^2 I = F^* \mathrm{diag}(S + \sigma^2) F$, and the gain $K$ is diagonal in the Fourier basis, as in Corollary 2.8. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The Wiener filter is optimal among all estimators when the image is Gaussian and stationary — which a photograph is not. One spectrum cannot describe both a flat sky and a textured roof: the global filter blurs the textures or leaves noise in the sky. Restricting the Gaussian model to small regions, the *patches*, is the step taken in ch. 4–6.

### 3.6 A handful of denoising principles

The course description groups the methods found since the 1970s into a few principles. Each one is a hypothesis on the redundancy of images.

| Principle | Representative methods | Hypothesis on the image |
|---|---|---|
| Local linear filtering | Gaussian filter; Wiener filter (Wiener, 1949) | smooth, or stationary Gaussian |
| Neighbourhood filters | Yaroslavsky (1985); bilateral filter (Tomasi and Manduchi, 1998) | nearby pixels of similar grey level share the same value |
| Variational and PDE methods | anisotropic diffusion (Perona and Malik, 1990); total variation (Rudin, Osher and Fatemi, 1992) | piecewise smooth, small total variation |
| Transform thresholding | wavelet shrinkage (Donoho and Johnstone, 1994); sliding DCT (Yu and Sapiro, 2011) | sparse in a fixed orthonormal basis |
| Non-local self-similarity | NL-means (Buades, Coll and Morel, 2005) | every patch has similar copies in the image |
| Bayesian patch models, collaborative filtering | BM3D (Dabov et al., 2007); EPLL (Zoran and Weiss, 2011); NL-Bayes (Lebrun, Buades and Morel, 2013) | groups of similar patches are Gaussian, or sparse in a 3D transform |
| Learned denoisers | MLP (Burger, Schuler and Harmeling, 2012); DnCNN (Zhang et al., 2017) | whatever is regular in a training set |

The survey by Lebrun, Colom, Buades and Morel (2012) analyses the classical methods as combinations of a few ingredients shared across principles. Three of them return in every later chapter: the *aggregation* of overlapping estimates, a second pass guided by a first *oracle* estimate, and the choice of a *patch model*.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::

-   PSNR is $10\log_{10}(255^2/\mathrm{MSE})$; the noisy image at $\sigma = 20$ scores 22.11 dB.
-   Noise limits the information per pixel (Shannon); denoising exploits the redundancy of images.
-   Camera noise is Poisson–Gaussian with an affine noise curve; the Anscombe transform makes it nearly Gaussian with unit variance.
-   The MAD of fine high-pass coefficients estimates $\sigma$; texture biases it upwards.
-   Gaussian filtering removes $\frac{h^2}{2}\Delta u$; the Wiener filter is optimal only for stationary Gaussian images.
::::

## 4. Multiscale DCT denoising {#ch4}

If the clean image is *sparse* in an orthonormal basis — few large coefficients — and the noise is spread evenly over all coefficients (Theorem 2.4), then keeping the large coefficients and killing the small ones separates the two. This chapter makes the idea quantitative, applies it to sliding DCT patches, and repairs its main defect with a multiscale scheme.

### 4.1 Thresholding in an orthonormal basis

In an orthonormal basis, the observation becomes $y_k = x_k + n_k$, $k = 1, \dots, d$, with independent $n_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ and unknown coefficients $x_k$ of the clean image.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Hard and soft thresholding]{.tag} For a threshold $\tau > 0$,

$$
\eta_H(y) = y\, \mathbf{1}[|y| > \tau], \qquad \eta_S(y) = \mathrm{sign}(y)\, (|y| - \tau)_+ .
$$

Hard thresholding keeps or kills; soft thresholding also shrinks the survivors by $\tau$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Two oracles]{.tag} Suppose an oracle reveals the $|x_k|$.

-   The best *keep-or-kill* estimator keeps $y_k$ exactly when $x_k^2 > \sigma^2$; its risk is $R_P = \sum_k \min(x_k^2, \sigma^2)$.
-   The best *attenuation* $a_k y_k$ uses $a_k = x_k^2/(x_k^2 + \sigma^2)$; its risk is $R_A = \sum_k \frac{x_k^2 \sigma^2}{x_k^2 + \sigma^2}$.

Moreover

$$
\tfrac12 R_P \ \le\ R_A \ \le\ R_P .
$$

::: proof
The risk of $a\, y_k$ is $(1 - a)^2 x_k^2 + a^2 \sigma^2$. Over $a \in \{0, 1\}$ the minimum is $\min(x_k^2, \sigma^2)$.

Over $a \in \mathbb{R}$, the minimum is attained at $a_k$ and equals $x_k^2\sigma^2/(x_k^2 + \sigma^2)$.

The right inequality holds because $\{0, 1\} \subset \mathbb{R}$. For the left one, write $x_k^2 \sigma^2 = \min \cdot \max$ and use $x_k^2 + \sigma^2 \le 2 \max$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The oracle risk counts the coefficients above the noise level. It is small exactly when the image is sparse in the basis: the choice of the basis is the hypothesis on the image.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — The maximum of the noise]{.tag} Let $\tau_d = \sigma\sqrt{2 \log d}$, the *universal threshold*. Then

$$
\mathbb{P}\Big(\max_{k \le d} |n_k| > \tau_d\Big) \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi \log d}} .
$$

::: proof
For $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $t > 0$, the Mills inequality gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(|Z| > t) \le \frac{2}{t\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-t^2/2}.
$$

A union bound over $d$ coefficients with $t = \sqrt{2 \log d}$ gives

$$
d \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt{2\log d}} \cdot \frac{1}{d} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi \log d}}.
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $\tau_d$, all pure-noise coefficients die with high probability, but slowly: for $d = 64$, $\tau_d = 2.88\sigma$ and the bound is 0.28.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Donoho–Johnstone (1994)]{.tag} Soft thresholding at the universal threshold $\tau_d$ satisfies

$$
\mathbb{E}\|\eta_S(y) - x\|^2 \ \le\ (2 \log d + 1)\Big(\sigma^2 + \sum_k \min(x_k^2, \sigma^2)\Big).
$$

::: proof
*Sketch*, with $\sigma = 1$. The scalar risk of soft thresholding satisfies $r(\tau, \mu) \le e^{-\tau^2/2} + \min(\mu^2, 1 + \tau^2)$; see Donoho and Johnstone (1994) or Mallat (2009, ch. 11).

With $\tau^2 = 2 \log d$ the first term is $1/d$. Summing over $k$ and using $\min(\mu^2, 1 + \tau^2) \le (1 + \tau^2) \min(\mu^2, 1)$ gives the bound. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Up to a factor $2\log d$, a simple rule matches the keep-or-kill oracle, and Donoho and Johnstone show that this factor cannot be improved asymptotically, uniformly over all signals. In practice the universal threshold is too high for the mean square error, and $\tau$ is tuned on the data.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — SURE for soft thresholding]{.tag} The quantity

$$
\mathrm{SURE}(\tau) = -d\sigma^2 + \sum_k \min(y_k^2, \tau^2) + 2\sigma^2\, \#\{k : |y_k| > \tau\}
$$

is an unbiased estimate of the risk $\mathbb{E}\|\eta_S(y) - x\|^2$.

::: proof
Apply Theorem 2.11 to $f = \eta_S$ coordinatewise. Here $|f(y_k) - y_k| = \min(|y_k|, \tau)$, and $f'(y_k) = \mathbf{1}[|y_k| > \tau]$ almost everywhere. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Minimising SURE over $\tau$ chooses the threshold from the noisy data alone (the *SureShrink* rule of Donoho and Johnstone, 1995). The code applies it to the global DCT of a $256 \times 256$ crop of `flower.jpg` with $\sigma = 20$.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import dctn
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
u = load_sample_image("flower.jpg").mean(axis=2)[:256, :256]
sigma = 20.0
x = dctn(u, norm="ortho").ravel()                        # clean coefficients
y = x + sigma * rng.standard_normal(x.size)              # noisy coefficients (Theorem 2.4)
d = y.size

def sure(t):    # Proposition 4.5, divided by d
    return (np.minimum(y**2, t**2).sum() - d * sigma**2 + 2 * sigma**2 * (np.abs(y) > t).sum()) / d

def true_mse(t):
    return ((np.sign(y) * np.maximum(np.abs(y) - t, 0) - x) ** 2).mean()

grid = sigma * np.array([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, np.sqrt(2 * np.log(d))])
for t in grid:
    print(f"tau = {t / sigma:4.2f} sigma: SURE {sure(t):6.1f}   true MSE {true_mse(t):6.1f}")
```

SURE follows the true error within 3 units on the whole grid. Both are minimal at $\tau = 1.5\sigma$ (MSE 70.2, i.e. 29.7 dB), while the universal threshold $4.71\sigma$ gives 131.6.

### 4.2 Sliding-window DCT denoising

A global basis adapts poorly to an image whose content changes from place to place. The DCT of *small* patches adapts to local content, and processing every patch position removes the dependence on a grid.

::: thm
[Algorithm 4.6 — Sliding-window DCT denoising (Yu and Sapiro, 2011)]{.tag}

1.  For every position, extract the $s \times s$ patch of $\tilde u$ ($s = 8$ or 16).
2.  Compute its 2D DCT and set to zero the coefficients with $|y| < 3\sigma$.
3.  Invert the DCT: this gives an estimate of the patch.
4.  Each pixel belongs to $s^2$ patches: *aggregate* by averaging its $s^2$ estimates.
:::

A pure-noise coefficient survives the threshold $3\sigma$ with probability 0.0027, about 0.17 coefficient per $8 \times 8$ patch.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — Aggregation never hurts]{.tag} If $\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_K$ are estimates of the same value $x$, then

$$
\Big(\frac1K \sum_j \hat x_j - x\Big)^2 \le \frac1K \sum_j (\hat x_j - x)^2 .
$$

::: proof
Convexity of the square (Jensen's inequality) applied to the errors $\hat x_j - x$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When the errors of overlapping patches are weakly correlated, the gain approaches a division by $K$. Averaging over all translations is the *cycle spinning* of Coifman and Donoho (1995).

### 4.3 Why one scale is not enough

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.8 — Residual low-frequency noise]{.tag} In a patch of $d$ pixels, the noise of the constant (DC) coefficient is $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ and this coefficient is almost always kept. It adds to every pixel of the patch an error of variance

$$
\sigma^2 / d .
$$

::: proof
The DC atom is the constant $1/\sqrt{d}$; its coefficient times the atom contributes (coefficient)$/\sqrt{d}$ to each pixel. Theorem 2.4 gives the law of the noise part. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The same holds for the few lowest frequencies, which survive in most patches. After aggregation these errors are smooth over about $s$ pixels: faint blotches, visible in flat regions although small in MSE. For $\sigma = 40$ and $8 \times 8$ patches, the DC error alone has standard deviation 5 grey levels.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.9 — A coarse scale is less noisy]{.tag} Keep the $\frac N2 \times \frac N2$ lowest coefficients of the orthonormal global DCT of an $N \times N$ image, invert at size $\frac N2$ and divide by 2. The result is a half-size version of the image whose noise is white with variance

$$
\sigma^2 / 4 .
$$

::: proof
The kept noise coefficients are independent $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ (Theorem 2.4). The orthonormal inverse at half size gives white noise of variance $\sigma^2$ again, and the division by 2 divides the variance by 4. The factor 2 preserves grey levels: a constant image $c$ has DC coefficient $cN$, which becomes the constant $2c$ at half size. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 4.4 The multiscale DCT

At the coarse scale, the slow variations of the image become fast, and the patches of the same size see them at a lower noise level. This motivates the following scheme, in the spirit of the *Multi-Scale DCT Denoising* of Pierazzo, Morel and Facciolo (2017); the code is a simplified version.

::: thm
[Algorithm 4.10 — Two-scale DCT denoising]{.tag}

1.  Build the coarse image $c$ of Proposition 4.9 (noise $\sigma/2$).
2.  Denoise $c$ and $\tilde u$ with Algorithm 4.6, at levels $\sigma/2$ and $\sigma$.
3.  In the global DCT of the fine estimate, replace the lowest frequencies — a fraction $r$ of the coarse band on each axis — by those of the coarse estimate.
4.  Invert. Applied recursively to $c$, the scheme gives a pyramid.
:::

The fraction $r$ trades the cleaner low frequencies of the coarse scale against the band-limiting artefacts of the half-size image; the code uses $r = 1/4$.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import dctn, idctn
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

def dct_denoise(f, sigma, s=8, thr=3.0):
    """Sliding-window DCT: hard thresholding at thr * sigma, uniform aggregation."""
    P = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(f, (s, s))   # every s x s patch
    C = dctn(P, axes=(-2, -1), norm="ortho")
    C[np.abs(C) < thr * sigma] = 0.0
    Q = idctn(C, axes=(-2, -1), norm="ortho")
    out, cnt = np.zeros_like(f), np.zeros_like(f)
    h, w = Q.shape[:2]
    for i in range(s):                                       # put every estimate back
        for j in range(s):
            out[i:i + h, j:j + w] += Q[:, :, i, j]
            cnt[i:i + h, j:j + w] += 1
    return out / cnt

def two_scale(f, sigma, r=0.25):
    """Coarse scale = low-frequency quarter of the global DCT, with noise sigma / 2."""
    F = dctn(f, norm="ortho")
    n = f.shape[0] // 2
    coarse = idctn(F[:n, :n], norm="ortho") / 2
    c_hat = dct_denoise(coarse, sigma / 2)
    G = dctn(dct_denoise(f, sigma), norm="ortho")
    k = int(r * n)
    G[:k, :k] = dctn(2 * c_hat, norm="ortho")[:k, :k]        # replace the lowest frequencies
    return idctn(G, norm="ortho")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
crops = {"china.jpg": (slice(100, 356), slice(200, 456)), "flower.jpg": (slice(0, 256), slice(0, 256))}
for name, sigma in [("china.jpg", 20.0), ("china.jpg", 40.0), ("flower.jpg", 20.0), ("flower.jpg", 40.0)]:
    u = load_sample_image(name).mean(axis=2)[crops[name]]
    f = u + sigma * rng.standard_normal(u.shape)
    psnr = lambda a: 10 * np.log10(255**2 / np.mean((a - u) ** 2))
    print(f"{name:10s} sigma {sigma:2.0f}: noisy {psnr(f):5.2f} | DCT {psnr(dct_denoise(f, sigma)):5.2f}"
          f" | two scales {psnr(two_scale(f, sigma)):5.2f} dB")
```

| Image, noise | Noisy | Sliding DCT | Two scales |
|---|---|---|---|
| `china.jpg` crop, $\sigma = 20$ | 22.12 | 26.78 | 26.81 |
| `china.jpg` crop, $\sigma = 40$ | 16.06 | 23.31 | 23.37 |
| `flower.jpg` crop, $\sigma = 20$ | 22.09 | 35.62 | 35.74 |
| `flower.jpg` crop, $\sigma = 40$ | 16.09 | 30.97 | 31.78 |

The local DCT beats the global SURE-tuned thresholding by 6 dB on the flower crop (35.62 against 29.7 dB). The second scale gains 0.8 dB where it matters — a smooth image at high noise — and almost nothing on the textured crop, as Proposition 4.8 predicts.

::: note
[IPOL experiment — DCT denoising]{.tag} Run the DCT denoising demo on IPOL on an image with large flat regions at $\sigma = 40$. Inspect the flat regions of the result: the low-frequency blotches of Proposition 4.8 are visible. Then compare with the multiscale DCT demo.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::

-   Thresholding works when the image is sparse and the noise spread evenly; the oracle risk counts the coefficients above $\sigma$.
-   The universal threshold $\sigma\sqrt{2\log d}$ kills all noise coefficients with high probability; SURE tunes $\tau$ from the noisy data.
-   Sliding-window DCT adapts to local content; aggregation of overlapping estimates never increases the error.
-   Patch methods leave low-frequency noise of variance $\sigma^2/d$; a coarse scale with noise $\sigma/2$ removes it.
::::

## 5. Image self-similarity and denoising {#ch5}

Transform thresholding assumes that each patch is sparse in a fixed basis. Self-similarity makes a different bet: most patches of an image have near copies elsewhere in the same image, and averaging these copies removes the noise without blurring. This chapter builds non-local means on this bet and studies the space of patches that makes it work.

### 5.1 From local to non-local averaging

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Neighbourhood filters]{.tag} The Yaroslavsky filter (1985) averages the pixels of a spatial neighbourhood $B(i, \rho)$ whose grey level is close to that of $i$:

$$
\mathrm{YNF}(\tilde u)(i) = \frac{1}{C(i)} \sum_{j \in B(i, \rho)} e^{-|\tilde u(i) - \tilde u(j)|^2 / h^2}\, \tilde u(j),
$$

where $C(i)$ normalises the weights. The bilateral filter (Tomasi and Manduchi, 1998) replaces the ball by a Gaussian spatial weight.
:::

The comparison of two single noisy grey levels is unreliable. The expected value of $|\tilde u(i) - \tilde u(j)|^2$ is $|u(i) - u(j)|^2 + 2\sigma^2$, with fluctuations of the same order as $2\sigma^2$. At $\sigma = 20$, two pixels that differ by 20 grey levels cannot be told apart. Comparing whole patches fixes this, thanks to the concentration of Proposition 2.5.

### 5.2 Non-local means

::: def
[Definition 5.2 — Non-local means (Buades, Coll and Morel, 2005)]{.tag} Let $\tilde P_i$ be the $s \times s$ noisy patch centred at $i$, with $d = s^2$ pixels, and

$$
\delta^2(i, j) = \frac1d \|\tilde P_i - \tilde P_j\|^2 .
$$

NL-means replaces $\tilde u(i)$ by a weighted average over a search window $W(i)$:

$$
\mathrm{NL}(\tilde u)(i) = \frac{\sum_{j \in W(i)} w(i,j)\, \tilde u(j)}{\sum_{j \in W(i)} w(i,j)}, \qquad w(i,j) = \exp\Big(-\frac{\max(\delta^2(i,j) - 2\sigma^2,\, 0)}{h^2}\Big).
$$
:::

The subtraction of $2\sigma^2$ and the parameter $h$ come from the statistics of the patch distance.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — Distance between noisy patches]{.tag} Let two non-overlapping patches differ by $\Delta = P_i - P_j$, with independent white noise. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}\,\|\tilde P_i - \tilde P_j\|^2 = \|\Delta\|^2 + 2d\sigma^2, \qquad \mathrm{Var}\,\|\tilde P_i - \tilde P_j\|^2 = 8\sigma^2 \|\Delta\|^2 + 8 d\sigma^4 .
$$

For identical patches, $\delta^2$ has mean $2\sigma^2$ and standard deviation $2\sqrt2\, \sigma^2 / \sqrt d$.

::: proof
$\tilde P_i - \tilde P_j = \Delta + M$ with $M \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2\sigma^2 I_d)$. The mean of $\|\Delta + M\|^2$ is $\|\Delta\|^2 + 2d\sigma^2$.

For the variance, write the centred distance as

$$
\|\Delta + M\|^2 - \|\Delta\|^2 - 2d\sigma^2 = 2\langle \Delta, M\rangle + \big(\|M\|^2 - 2d\sigma^2\big).
$$

The two terms are uncorrelated, since odd moments of $M$ vanish. Their variances are $4 \cdot 2\sigma^2\|\Delta\|^2$ and $2d(2\sigma^2)^2$ (Proposition 2.5). Divide by $d$ for $\delta^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.4 — Choosing $h$]{.tag} Take $\sigma = 20$ and $5 \times 5$ patches ($d = 25$). Identical patches have $\delta^2 = 800$ on average, with standard deviation

$$
2\sqrt2 \times 400 / 5 = 226 .
$$

Subtracting $2\sigma^2$ centres the distance of true copies at zero. A filtering parameter $h = 0.7\sigma$ gives $h^2 = 196$, about one standard deviation: true copies keep weights near 1, while patches that differ by more than a few standard deviations get negligible weights.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — NL-means estimates a conditional expectation (sketch)]{.tag} Model the noisy image as a stationary random field with a mixing condition (distant regions nearly independent). Buades, Coll and Morel (2005) show that, as the image size grows and $h \to 0$ suitably, the NL-means value at $i$ converges to the conditional expectation of the noisy centre $\tilde u(i)$ given the noisy neighbourhood $\tilde u(N_i)$, with the centre excluded from $N_i$.

*Why this is the right target.* The noise $n(i)$ is independent of $\tilde u(N_i)$ and centred, so

$$
\mathbb{E}[\tilde u(i) \mid \tilde u(N_i)] = \mathbb{E}[u(i) \mid \tilde u(N_i)] .
$$

The limit is the MMSE estimate of the clean pixel from its noisy surroundings (Theorem 0.5).

*Key step of the proof.* NL-means is a Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression of $\tilde u(i)$ on the neighbourhoods, and kernel regression is consistent for stationary mixing data.
:::

The identity above — a noisy value is an unbiased target for a predictor that does not see it — reappears in the self-supervised denoisers of ch. 10.

The code implements Definition 5.2 with $5 \times 5$ patches, a $21 \times 21$ window and $h = 0.7\sigma$, on the crop of ch. 4.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import uniform_filter, gaussian_filter
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
u = load_sample_image("china.jpg").mean(axis=2)[100:356, 200:456]
sigma = 20.0
f = u + sigma * rng.standard_normal(u.shape)
psnr = lambda a: 10 * np.log10(255**2 / np.mean((a - u) ** 2))

def nl_means(f, sigma, half_patch=2, half_win=10, h=0.7):
    """Pixelwise NL-means (Definition 5.2), vectorised over the offsets of the window."""
    r = half_win
    g = np.pad(f, r, mode="reflect")
    num, den = np.zeros_like(f), np.zeros_like(f)
    for dx in range(-r, r + 1):
        for dy in range(-r, r + 1):
            shifted = g[r + dx: r + dx + f.shape[0], r + dy: r + dy + f.shape[1]]
            # mean squared distance between the patches centred at i and at i + (dx, dy)
            d2 = uniform_filter((f - shifted) ** 2, size=2 * half_patch + 1, mode="reflect")
            w = np.exp(-np.maximum(d2 - 2 * sigma**2, 0.0) / (h * sigma) ** 2)
            num += w * shifted
            den += w
    return num / den

best = max((psnr(gaussian_filter(f, s)), s) for s in [0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 1.0])
print(f"noisy {psnr(f):.2f} dB | best Gaussian {best[0]:.2f} dB (h = {best[1]})"
      f" | NL-means 5x5 / 21x21 {psnr(nl_means(f, sigma)):.2f} dB")
```

NL-means reaches 27.01 dB against 24.59 dB for the best Gaussian filter and 26.78 dB for the sliding DCT of ch. 4. The weights adapt to the image: on a straight edge, the similar patches lie along the edge, and the average does not cross it.

### 5.3 Method noise and parameters

The method noise of NL-means (Definition 3.8) is close to white noise on textured and periodic images, where many exact copies exist. Its parameters act as follows.

-   **$h$ too small**: only the central patch has a large weight, and noise remains.
-   **$h$ too large**: dissimilar patches enter the average, and details blur.
-   **Window size**: a larger window finds more copies but also more false matches, and costs more.
-   **Rare patches** — corners, ends of lines, unique details — have few copies. They are barely denoised: this is the *rare patch effect*, and the main residual defect of the method.

::: note
[IPOL experiment — NL-means]{.tag} Run the NL-means demo on IPOL at $\sigma = 10, 30, 60$. Look at the method noise $\tilde u - \mathrm{NL}(\tilde u)$: where does it contain structure? Relate the answer to the rare patch effect.
:::

### 5.4 The space of patches

The objectives of the course single out patches from $8 \times 8$ to $60 \times 60$ pixels. Two facts govern their use: larger patches are compared more reliably, and larger patches have fewer copies.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.6 — Patch size and discrimination]{.tag} Declare two noisy patches different when $\delta^2 - 2\sigma^2$ exceeds $k$ standard deviations of its value for identical patches. Two patches with mean squared difference $\bar\Delta^2 = \|\Delta\|^2 / d$ are separated, on average, when

$$
\bar\Delta^2 \ \ge\ \frac{2\sqrt2\, k\, \sigma^2}{\sqrt d}.
$$

::: proof
By Proposition 5.3, $\delta^2 - 2\sigma^2$ has mean $\bar\Delta^2$, and for identical patches its standard deviation is $2\sqrt2\sigma^2 / \sqrt d$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For $\sigma = 20$ and $k = 3$, an $8 \times 8$ patch separates differences of root mean square $\bar\Delta \approx 20.6$ grey levels, and a $60 \times 60$ patch separates $\bar\Delta \approx 7.5$.

But a $60 \times 60$ region rarely has a copy in the same image. Every patch method chooses a size between these two constraints, and deep networks face the same trade-off with their receptive field (ch. 7.5).

The global ensemble of patches is far from filling its space. Natural $3 \times 3$ patches of high contrast concentrate near a two-dimensional manifold of edges (Lee, Pedersen and Mumford, 2003), whose topology is that of a Klein bottle (Carlsson, Ishkhanov, de Silva and Zomorodian, 2008). Small patches recur within the same image, at the same and at other scales (Zontak and Irani, 2011).

The PCA of all the patches of an image gives a first, linear, picture of this structure. The number of principal variances above $\sigma^2$ is the number of directions that a Wiener filter keeps (Corollary 2.8).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

u = load_sample_image("china.jpg").mean(axis=2)
for s in [4, 8, 16]:
    P = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(u, (s, s))[::2, ::2].reshape(-1, s * s)
    lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(np.cov(P, rowvar=False))[::-1]       # patch PCA spectrum
    above = [int((lam > sig**2).sum()) for sig in (5, 20, 40)]
    print(f"{s:2d}x{s:<2d} (d = {s*s:3d}): top eigenvalues {np.round(lam[:3]).astype(int)},"
          f" eigenvalues above sigma^2 for sigma = 5, 20, 40: {above}")
```

| Patch size | $d$ | Eigenvalues above $\sigma^2$: $\sigma = 5$ | $\sigma = 20$ | $\sigma = 40$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $4 \times 4$ | 16 | 16 | 7 | 1 |
| $8 \times 8$ | 64 | 64 | 30 | 7 |
| $16 \times 16$ | 256 | 256 | 116 | 24 |

At $\sigma = 40$ a global Gaussian model keeps only 7 of the 64 directions of an $8 \times 8$ patch, the same for every patch. Groups of *similar* patches have a much lower dimension and their own principal axes: ch. 6 builds one Gaussian model per group.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::

-   Neighbourhood filters compare single grey levels and fail at moderate noise; NL-means compares patches.
-   The squared distance of noisy patches is biased by $2d\sigma^2$ and fluctuates by $2\sqrt2\sigma^2/\sqrt d$ per pixel: subtract the bias, set $h$ near the fluctuation.
-   NL-means is a kernel regression that converges to the MMSE estimate of a pixel given its noisy neighbourhood.
-   Large patches discriminate better but have fewer copies; rare patches are poorly denoised.
-   Patches of natural images occupy a small part of their space: few principal directions survive the noise.
::::

## 6. Bayesian patch-based methods {#ch6}

NL-means averages similar patches with scalar weights. A group of similar patches carries more information: its mean and its covariance. This chapter models each group as a Gaussian vector and applies the Wiener estimator of ch. 2 to it. The result, NL-Bayes, and its sibling BM3D are among the best classical denoisers.

### 6.1 A Gaussian model for groups of similar patches

Collect $K$ noisy patches $\tilde P_1, \dots, \tilde P_K$ similar to a reference patch, with $d$ pixels each. Model the clean patches as independent draws of $\mathcal{N}(m, C)$ and the noise as white.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.1 — Moments of a noisy group]{.tag} With $\tilde m$ the sample mean and $\tilde C$ the unbiased sample covariance of the noisy group,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\tilde m] = m, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\tilde C] = C + \sigma^2 I .
$$

::: proof
The noisy patches are independent with mean $m$ and covariance $C + \sigma^2 I$, since signal and noise are independent (Proposition 0.2). The sample mean and the unbiased sample covariance of independent draws are unbiased. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — The empirical Bayes patch estimator]{.tag} Replace $m$ by $\tilde m$ and $C$ by $\tilde C - \sigma^2 I$ in the Wiener estimator of Theorem 2.7. If $\tilde C - \sigma^2 I$ is positive semi-definite, the estimate of each patch of the group is

::: key
[Key result — NL-Bayes, first step]{.tag}

$$
\hat P = \tilde P - \sigma^2\, \tilde C^{-1} (\tilde P - \tilde m)
$$
:::

In the eigenbasis of $\tilde C$, with eigenvalues $\mu_i$, it multiplies the $i$-th coefficient of $\tilde P - \tilde m$ by $1 - \sigma^2/\mu_i$.

In practice the factor is clipped to $(1 - \sigma^2/\mu_i)_+$, which handles the directions where $\mu_i < \sigma^2$.

::: proof
With $C = \tilde C - \sigma^2 I$, we have $C + \sigma^2 I = \tilde C$, hence

$$
C(C + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} = I - \sigma^2 \tilde C^{-1} .
$$

Substituting in $\tilde m + C(C + \sigma^2 I)^{-1}(\tilde P - \tilde m)$ gives the formula. The eigenvalues of $I - \sigma^2\tilde C^{-1}$ are $1 - \sigma^2/\mu_i$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The estimator is a PCA of the group followed by a Wiener shrinkage: directions where the group varies more than the noise are kept, the others are attenuated. Unlike the DCT, the basis is *adapted* to each group.

When $K$ is not much larger than $d$, the sample eigenvalues are noisy. For pure noise, as $d, K \to \infty$ with $d/K \to \gamma < 1$, the eigenvalues of $\tilde C$ spread over the interval of Marchenko and Pastur (1967):

$$
\big[\sigma^2 (1 - \sqrt\gamma)^2,\ \sigma^2 (1 + \sqrt\gamma)^2\big].
$$

::: ex
[Example 6.3 — Noise that looks like signal]{.tag} With $5 \times 5$ patches ($d = 25$) and $K = 60$ similar patches, $\gamma = 0.42$ and the interval is $[0.13\sigma^2, 2.71\sigma^2]$. A pure-noise direction can show $\mu_i = 2.7\sigma^2$, and its shrinkage factor is then

$$
1 - 1/2.7 = 0.63 :
$$

63 % of the noise in that direction survives. A second step with a better covariance estimate is needed.
:::

### 6.2 NL-Bayes

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.4 — NL-Bayes (Lebrun, Buades and Morel, 2013), simplified]{.tag}

1.  **Step 1.** For each reference patch (on a grid of step $p$), find the $K$ most similar patches in a search window. Estimate $\tilde m$ and $\tilde C$, apply Theorem 6.2 with clipped factors to *every* patch of the group, and aggregate all the estimates by averaging. This gives a basic estimate $\hat u_1$.
2.  **Step 2 (oracle).** Redo the grouping on $\hat u_1$, whose patch distances are far less noisy. Estimate the covariance $C_1$ from the basic patches, and apply the Wiener estimate with $C = C_1$ to the *noisy* patches. Aggregate.
:::

The full algorithm adds a test for flat groups — if the group variance is close to $\sigma^2$, every patch is replaced by the mean — and works on colour patches. The code below keeps the two steps.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
u = load_sample_image("china.jpg").mean(axis=2)[100:356, 200:456]
sigma = 20.0
f = u + sigma * rng.standard_normal(u.shape)
psnr = lambda a: 10 * np.log10(255**2 / np.mean((a - u) ** 2))

def nl_bayes_step(f, guide, sigma, s=5, K=60, win=10, stride=4, oracle=False):
    """One step of a simplified NL-Bayes: group, Gaussian (Wiener) estimate, aggregate."""
    H, W = f.shape
    view = lambda a: np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(a, (s, s)).reshape(H - s + 1, W - s + 1, -1)
    Pf, Pg = view(f), view(guide)
    off = (np.arange(s)[:, None] * W + np.arange(s)[None, :]).ravel()   # pixel offsets in a patch
    out, cnt = np.zeros(H * W), np.zeros(H * W)
    rows = sorted(set(range(0, H - s + 1, stride)) | {H - s})
    cols = sorted(set(range(0, W - s + 1, stride)) | {W - s})
    for i in rows:
        for j in cols:
            i0, i1 = max(i - win, 0), min(i + win, H - s) + 1
            j0, j1 = max(j - win, 0), min(j + win, W - s) + 1
            d2 = ((Pg[i0:i1, j0:j1] - Pg[i, j]) ** 2).sum(-1).ravel()
            idx = np.argpartition(d2, K)[:K]                  # the K most similar patches
            ii, jj = np.unravel_index(idx, (i1 - i0, j1 - j0))
            ii, jj = ii + i0, jj + j0
            Y, m = Pf[ii, jj], Pf[ii, jj].mean(0)               # noisy group (K x d) and its mean
            if oracle:   # step 2: covariance of the basic estimate
                C = np.cov(Pg[ii, jj], rowvar=False)
            else:        # step 1: Cov(noisy) - sigma^2 I, eigenvalues clipped at 0
                lam, U = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(Y, rowvar=False))
                C = (U * np.maximum(lam - sigma**2, 0)) @ U.T
            Wf = C @ np.linalg.inv(C + sigma**2 * np.eye(s * s))  # Wiener matrix
            est = m + (Y - m) @ Wf.T
            pix = ((ii * W + jj)[:, None] + off[None, :]).ravel()
            np.add.at(out, pix, est.ravel())                  # aggregate every estimated patch
            np.add.at(cnt, pix, 1.0)
    return (out / cnt).reshape(H, W)

basic = nl_bayes_step(f, f, sigma)
final = nl_bayes_step(f, basic, sigma, oracle=True)
print(f"noisy {psnr(f):.2f} dB | step 1 {psnr(basic):.2f} dB | step 2 {psnr(final):.2f} dB")
```

The first step reaches 27.33 dB on the crop of ch. 4 ($\sigma = 20$), and the oracle step 27.75 dB, above NL-means (27.01 dB) and the sliding DCT (26.78 dB). The second step gains 0.4 dB because the covariance of the basic estimate is no longer inflated by noise eigenvalues (Example 6.3).

::: note
[IPOL experiment — NL-Bayes and BM3D]{.tag} Run the IPOL implementations of NL-Bayes and BM3D on the same noisy image at $\sigma = 20$ and $\sigma = 50$. Compare the basic and final estimates when the demo displays both, and look for residual low-frequency noise (Proposition 4.8) in flat regions.
:::

### 6.3 BM3D as a collaborative Wiener filter

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — BM3D (Dabov, Foi, Katkovnik and Egiazarian, 2007)]{.tag} For each reference patch:

1.  *block matching*: stack the most similar patches into a 3D group;
2.  apply a fixed separable 3D transform — a 2D transform on each patch, then a 1D transform across the group;
3.  step 1: hard-threshold the 3D coefficients; step 2: multiply each noisy coefficient $y_k$ by the empirical Wiener factor $\hat b_k^2 / (\hat b_k^2 + \sigma^2)$, where $\hat b_k$ is the coefficient of the step-1 estimate;
4.  invert and aggregate all the patch estimates, with weights that favour sparse groups.
:::

Step 2 is the oracle attenuation of Proposition 4.2, with the unknown coefficients $x_k$ replaced by the pilot estimate $\hat b_k$. NL-Bayes and BM3D share the same skeleton — group, estimate jointly, aggregate, repeat with an oracle. They differ in the basis: fixed for BM3D, the PCA of the group for NL-Bayes. The *collaborative* filtering of BM3D thus exploits both sparsity (ch. 4) and self-similarity (ch. 5).

### 6.4 Learned patch priors: Gaussian mixtures and EPLL

NL-Bayes learns one Gaussian per group from the noisy image itself: an *internal* prior. One can instead learn a prior on patches from a database of clean images: an *external* prior.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.6 — MMSE estimate under a Gaussian mixture]{.tag} Let the prior be $p(P) = \sum_k \pi_k\, \mathcal{N}(P; m_k, C_k)$ and $\tilde P = P + N$ with white noise. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}[P \mid \tilde P] = \sum_k \gamma_k(\tilde P)\, \Big(m_k + C_k (C_k + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} (\tilde P - m_k)\Big),
$$

with responsibilities summing to 1,

$$
\gamma_k(\tilde P) \propto \pi_k\, \mathcal{N}(\tilde P;\, m_k,\, C_k + \sigma^2 I).
$$

::: proof
Introduce the hidden component label $Z$. Given $Z = k$, $(P, \tilde P)$ is Gaussian, and Theorem 2.7 gives the inner Wiener estimate.

The marginal of $\tilde P$ given $Z = k$ is $\mathcal{N}(m_k, C_k + \sigma^2 I)$, so Bayes' rule gives $\mathbb{P}(Z = k \mid \tilde P) = \gamma_k(\tilde P)$. The tower property averages over $Z$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The MMSE estimate is a *mixture of Wiener filters*, each selected softly by how well its component explains the noisy patch. Keeping only the most likely component gives a piecewise linear estimator (Yu, Sapiro and Mallat, 2012).

The EPLL method of Zoran and Weiss (2011) learns a Gaussian mixture with about two hundred components on $8 \times 8$ patches of natural images. It then computes a whole image $\hat u$ by approximately solving

$$
\min_u\ \frac{\lambda}{2}\|u - \tilde u\|^2 - \sum_i \log p(R_i u),
$$

where $R_i$ extracts the patch at $i$. The solver alternates a patch step (the Wiener filter of the most likely component) and an image step (a closed-form aggregation), while the weight of the patch term grows.

A Gaussian mixture learned on a database is a small statistical model trained on examples. The networks of ch. 7–8 take the same path with millions of parameters.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 6
:::

-   A group of similar noisy patches gives estimates of a local mean and of $C + \sigma^2 I$.
-   The empirical Wiener estimate $\tilde P - \sigma^2\tilde C^{-1}(\tilde P - \tilde m)$ is a PCA of the group with shrinkage $(1 - \sigma^2/\mu_i)_+$.
-   Sample eigenvalues of noise spread up to $\sigma^2(1 + \sqrt{d/K})^2$: a second, oracle step fixes the covariance.
-   BM3D uses a fixed 3D transform where NL-Bayes uses the group PCA; both group, estimate, aggregate and iterate.
-   Under a Gaussian-mixture prior, the MMSE estimate is a mixture of Wiener filters; EPLL learns such a prior from data.
::::

## 7. A crash course on deep learning {#ch7}

Since 2016, the best denoisers have been neural networks trained on examples. This chapter introduces them from scratch, as the official course does. Part I (ch. 7.1–7.4) covers networks, losses, gradients and optimisation; part II (ch. 7.5–7.7) covers convolutional networks and the training of a denoiser.

### 7.1 Neurons, layers and networks

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Multilayer perceptron]{.tag} With weight matrices $W_\ell$, biases $b_\ell$ and the rectified linear unit $\rho(t) = \max(t, 0)$ applied coordinatewise, a network of depth $L$ computes

$$
f_\theta(y) = W_L\, \rho\big(W_{L-1}\, \rho(\cdots \rho(W_1 y + b_1) \cdots) + b_{L-1}\big) + b_L .
$$

The parameters $\theta$ are all the $W_\ell$ and $b_\ell$; the intermediate vectors are the *hidden layers*.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — ReLU networks are piecewise linear, and conversely in 1D]{.tag} Every ReLU network is a continuous piecewise linear function. Conversely, every continuous piecewise linear $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with breakpoints $x_1 < \dots < x_n$ is a network with one hidden layer of $n + 2$ units.

::: proof
Affine maps and $\rho$ are continuous and piecewise linear, and so are their compositions.

For the converse, let $s_0$ be the slope of $g$ left of $x_1$ and $s_k$ its slope on $(x_k, x_{k+1})$. Then

$$
g(x) = g(x_1) + s_0\big(\rho(x - x_1) - \rho(x_1 - x)\big) + \sum_{k=1}^n (s_k - s_{k-1})\, \rho(x - x_k).
$$

Both sides are continuous, agree at $x_1$ and have the same slope on every interval, so they coincide. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Continuous functions on an interval are uniform limits of piecewise linear interpolants, so one hidden layer approximates any of them. This is the 1D case of the *universal approximation theorem* (Cybenko, 1989, for sigmoids; Leshno, Lin, Pinkus and Schocken, 1993, for every non-polynomial activation).
